title: Length and Data
bigQuestion: How can we measure how long something is and show what we found?

story.title: The Hallway in Shoes
story.kicker: A class measures the same hallway two ways and gets two very different numbers.
paragraphs: Ms. Ruiz's class had a question. How long is the hallway outside the room? Nobody knew. Amir had an idea. He took off one shoe. He set it on the floor by the wall. Then he set his other shoe in front of it, heel to toe.

Amir walked the hallway shoe by shoe. His friends counted with him. At the far wall he stopped. The count was 40 shoes. Then Nia tried it with her shoes. Her shoes were smaller. Her count was 50 shoes. The class was puzzled.

Ms. Ruiz brought out a long tape measure. It had numbers on it. Two students held the ends. They read the number at the far wall. The hallway was 30 feet long. Every student got 30 feet, no matter who held the tape.
Amir looked at the two numbers. Forty shoes. Fifty shoes. Thirty feet. The hallway had not changed at all. Only the unit had changed. That afternoon the class made a graph of everyone's shoe lengths.
story.think: Why did Amir and Nia get different numbers for the same hallway?

lessons.title: Longer and Shorter
lessons.mainIdea: To compare two lengths, line up one end, then look at the other end.
reading: Maya has a red crayon and a blue crayon. Which one is *longer*? She puts them side by side. She lines up the left ends. Now she looks at the right ends. The red crayon sticks out more. So the red crayon is longer. The blue crayon is *shorter*.
Lining up the ends matters. If one crayon starts ahead, you get fooled. A short crayon can look long. Always start both objects at the same line. Then compare the other ends.
Try it with a pencil and a marker. Line up the ends. Which one sticks out? That one is longer. If neither one sticks out, they are the same length.

words.d: reaching farther than the other object when the ends are lined up
not reaching as far as the other object when the ends are lined up

look.title: Two Pencils on a Desk
look.text: Picture two pencils on a desk. Their left ends touch the same line. The yellow pencil ends at the 4 on a ruler. The green pencil ends at the 6. Neither pencil has been moved.
look.prompt: Which pencil is longer? How do you know?

check.q: Two ribbons start at the same line. The blue ribbon sticks out past the red one. Which ribbon is longer?
check.why: The ends are lined up, so the ribbon that sticks out farther is longer. That is the blue one.

check.q: Why do you line up the ends before you compare?
check.why: If one object starts ahead, it looks longer than it is. Lining up the ends makes it fair.

check.q: A pencil is longer than a crayon. The crayon is longer than an eraser. Which is shortest?
check.why: Pencil is longer than crayon, and crayon is longer than eraser. So the eraser is the shortest of the three.

lessons.title: Putting Three in Order
lessons.mainIdea: Order lengths from shortest to longest by comparing two at a time.
reading: Leo has three sticks. The brown stick is 5 cubes long. The gray stick is 8 cubes long. The white stick is 3 cubes long. He wants to line them up from shortest to longest.
Compare two at a time. 3 is less than 5, so white goes before brown. 5 is less than 8, so brown goes before gray. The *order* is white, brown, gray. Shortest to longest: 3, 5, 8.
You can also order without numbers. Line up the ends. Find the shortest one. Set it first. Then find the next shortest. Keep going until all of them are in a row.

words.d: a line-up that goes from shortest to longest, or longest to shortest

look.title: Leo's Three Sticks
look.cite: Leo's sticks, measured in one-inch cubes (example)
look.prompt: Which stick is in the middle when you put them in order?

check.q: Three ropes are 4 feet, 9 feet and 6 feet long. Which order is shortest to longest?
check.why: 4 is less than 6, and 6 is less than 9. So the order is 4, 6, 9.

check.q: A jump rope is 7 feet. A scarf is 3 feet. A ladder is 10 feet. Which is longest?
check.why: 10 is more than 7 and more than 3. The ladder, at 10 feet, is longest.

check.q: Sam's pencil is longer than Ana's. Ana's pencil is longer than Kim's. Whose pencil is in the middle?
check.why: Sam's is longest and Kim's is shortest. Ana's is between them, so it is in the middle.

lessons.title: Units End to End
lessons.mainIdea: Measure by laying same-size units end to end with no gaps and no overlaps.
reading: How long is the book? Rosa uses paper clips. She lays them in a line along the edge. Each clip touches the next. No *gap*. No overlap. She counts 6 clips. The book is 6 paper clips long.
The clips must all be the same size. Big and small clips mixed give a wrong count. Gaps make the count too small. Overlaps make it too big. Start at one end. Stop at the other end.
A different *unit* gives a different number. The same book is 6 big clips long. It is 9 small clips long. The book did not change. The unit changed. A smaller unit means more units.

words.d: the one thing you use over and over to measure, like a paper clip or a cube
an empty space between two units that should be touching

look.title: Two Ways to Lay Cubes
look.text: Look at a crayon box. Ben lays 4 cubes along it, end to end, with no gaps. Jo lays 4 cubes too, but she leaves spaces between them. Her cubes reach past the end of the box.

check.q: Tia measures a shelf with cubes. She leaves gaps between the cubes. What happens to her count?
check.why: Gaps take up space that no cube covers. Fewer cubes fit, so the count is too small.

check.q: A desk is 5 long shoes long. You measure it again with short shoes. What happens?
check.why: Short shoes cover less space each. It takes more of them to reach the end of the desk.

check.q: Which rule is a good rule for measuring?
check.why: Same-size units that touch end to end give a true count. Gaps and mixed sizes give wrong counts.

lessons.title: Inches and Feet
lessons.mainIdea: An inch is a small unit. A foot is 12 inches. Use a ruler to measure.
reading: A *ruler* has marks. Each mark is one *inch*. Put the 0 end at one end of the object. Read the number at the other end. A marker ends at the 7. The marker is 7 inches long.
A *foot* is 12 inches. Your math book is about 1 foot long. A door is about 7 feet tall. Use inches for small things. Use feet for big things, like a rug or a room.
Do not start at the 1 mark. Start at 0. If you start at 1, your number is one too big. A crayon that ends at 5 looks like 5 inches. But it is only 4 inches.

words.d: a small unit of length; a paper clip is about 1 inch long
a unit of length equal to 12 inches; a math book is about 1 foot
a flat stick with marks for measuring inches or centimeters

look.title: Feet and Inches
look.prompt: How many inches are in 2 feet? How do you know?

check.q: A pencil starts at 0 on a ruler and ends at the 6. How long is it?
check.why: Starting at 0 and ending at 6 means 6 inches. From 0 to 6 is 6 inch marks.

check.q: How many inches are in 1 foot?
check.why: One foot is 12 inches. A 12-inch ruler is exactly one foot long.

check.q: Which is best measured in feet?
check.why: A rug is big. Feet are the bigger unit, so feet fit a rug. Clips and crayons use inches.

lessons.title: Centimeters and Meters
lessons.mainIdea: A centimeter is smaller than an inch. A meter is 100 centimeters.
reading: A *centimeter* is a small unit. It is about the width of your pinky finger. Many rulers show centimeters on one side. A paper clip is about 3 centimeters long.
A *meter* is 100 centimeters. A baseball bat is about 1 meter long. A door is about 2 meters tall. Use a meter stick for big things. Use a centimeter ruler for small things.
Measure a pencil twice. In inches it is 6. In centimeters it is 15. Centimeters are smaller, so you need more of them. Both numbers are right. They just use different units.

words.d: a small unit of length, about the width of a pinky finger
a unit of length equal to 100 centimeters, about one big step

look.title: One Book, Two Numbers
look.text: Nadia measures a book twice. With the inch side of the ruler, it is 10 inches. With the centimeter side, it is 25 centimeters. The book did not grow between the two measurements.
look.prompt: Why is the centimeter number bigger than the inch number?

check.q: How many centimeters are in 1 meter?
check.why: One meter is 100 centimeters. A meter stick has 100 centimeter marks.

check.q: A ribbon is 4 inches long. You measure it again in centimeters. What happens to the number?
check.why: A centimeter is smaller than an inch. It takes more centimeters to cover the ribbon, so the number is bigger.

check.q: Which tool is best for measuring a hallway?
check.why: A hallway is long. A meter stick is the biggest tool here, so it takes the fewest moves.

lessons.title: Estimate, Then Measure
lessons.mainIdea: An estimate is a careful guess. Use something you know as a guide.
reading: An *estimate* is a careful guess. You know a paper clip is about 1 inch. A crayon looks about 4 clips long. So your estimate is about 4 inches. Then you measure. It is 4 inches. Good estimate!
Big things need a bigger guide. Your math book is about 1 foot. A desk looks like 2 books. Estimate: about 2 feet. Then measure it. If it is 2 feet, your guess was close.
Estimates do not have to be exact. Close is good. If you guess 20 feet and it is 3 feet, think again. Pick a better guide. Then guess again.

words.d: a careful guess about a size or amount, made before you measure

look.title: Good Guides for Guessing
look.cite: Everyday classroom objects, rounded to the nearest inch
look.prompt: A desk looks like 3 rulers long. About how many inches is that?

check.q: A paper clip is about 1 inch. A marker looks like 5 clips long. About how long is the marker?
check.why: 5 clips at about 1 inch each is about 5 inches. Feet would be far too big for a marker.

check.q: What is an estimate?
check.why: An estimate is a careful guess you make before measuring. It does not have to be exact.

check.q: A rug looks like 6 math books long. A math book is about 1 foot. About how long is the rug?
check.why: 6 books at about 1 foot each is about 6 feet.

lessons.title: Picture Graphs and Bar Graphs
lessons.mainIdea: A graph shows counts with pictures or bars so you can compare fast.
reading: The class votes on a favorite pet. Dog gets 6 votes. Cat gets 4. Fish gets 2. A *picture graph* shows one picture for each vote. The dog row has 6 pictures. The cat row has 4.
A *bar graph* uses bars instead of pictures. A taller bar means more. The dog bar goes up to 6. The fish bar goes up to 2. You can see the winner fast. Dog wins.
Graphs answer questions. How many more dogs than cats? 6 − 4 = 2. How many votes in all? 6 + 4 + 2 = 12. Read the numbers off the graph. Then add or subtract.

words.d: a graph that uses one small picture for each thing counted
a graph that uses bars; a taller or longer bar means a bigger count

look.title: Favorite Pet Votes
look.prompt: How many more votes did dog get than fish?

check.q: A graph shows dog 6, cat 4, fish 2. How many more dogs than cats?
check.why: 6 − 4 = 2. Adding gives 10, which is a different question.

check.q: Dog 6, cat 4, fish 2. How many votes in all?
check.why: 6 + 4 = 10, then 10 + 2 = 12 votes in all.

check.q: In a bar graph, which bar shows the biggest count?
check.why: Bars grow with the count. The tallest bar stands for the biggest number.

lessons.title: Line Plots
lessons.mainIdea: A line plot puts an X above each measurement on a number line.
reading: The class measures pencils in inches. The lengths are 5, 6, 6, 7, 6, 5. A *line plot* shows them. Draw a number line from 5 to 7. Put an X above the number for each pencil.
Above 5 there are 2 X's. Above 6 there are 3 X's. Above 7 there is 1 X. The tallest stack shows the most common length. That is 6 inches.
Count all the X's to find how many pencils. 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 pencils. How many pencils are longer than 5 inches? Count the X's above 6 and 7. 3 + 1 = 4.

words.d: a number line with an X above a number for each measurement

look.title: Pencil Lengths
look.prompt: How many pencils are shorter than 7 inches?

check.q: A line plot has 2 X's above 5, 3 above 6 and 1 above 7. Which length is most common?
check.why: The tallest stack is above 6, with 3 X's. So 6 inches is most common.

check.q: Same plot: 2 X's above 5, 3 above 6, 1 above 7. How many pencils in all?
check.why: 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 pencils.

check.q: Same plot. How many pencils are longer than 5 inches?
check.why: Longer than 5 means the X's above 6 and 7. 3 + 1 = 4.

review.q: Two straws start at the same line. The green straw sticks out past the pink one. Which straw is shorter?
review.why: The green straw reaches farther, so it is longer. The pink straw is shorter.

review.q: Ivan measures a table with cubes. He leaves gaps between them. What is his count?
review.why: Gaps leave space with no cube in it. Fewer cubes fit, so the count is too small.

review.q: How many inches are in 1 foot?
review.why: One foot is 12 inches. 100 is centimeters in a meter.

review.q: A pencil is 6 inches long. You measure it in centimeters. The new number is...
review.why: Centimeters are smaller than inches, so more of them fit. The number is bigger, about 15.

review.q: A bar graph shows red 5, blue 3, green 4. How many votes in all?
A line plot has 1 X above 4, 4 X's above 5 and 2 X's above 6. Which length is most common?
review.why: The tallest stack is above 5, with 4 X's.
